Skybound - The Take off

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche: Strapped to a motor, lifted by a wing—meet the daring pilots pushing paramotoring to new limits, soaring where no one thought possible.

Unique Selling Point:
A first-hand look at the thrill and danger of cross-country paramotoring, as daring pilots defy the impossible—soaring across South Africa with nothing but a wing, a motor, and sheer determination.

Summary:
**Summary:**
Paramotoring—pure flight with nothing but a motor on your back and a wing above. It’s thrilling, it’s dangerous, and for a handful of South Africans, it’s an obsession. Meet Jean-Pierre Seger and Lawrence Marais, two pilots pushing the limits of what’s possible. From flying the first-ever paramotor journey from Joburg to Cape Town to planning an even greater challenge—crossing South Africa from north to south. With the sky as their only road and the wind as their greatest ally—or worst enemy—this is a test of endurance, skill, and survival. Our presenter takes to the skies to experience it firsthand, uncovering the risks, the freedom, and the sheer adrenaline of powered flight.

Further information:
**Further Information:**

Paramotoring is one of the most accessible forms of powered flight, requiring only a motorized backpack and a parachute-like wing to take off. But cross-country paramotoring is an entirely different challenge—demanding endurance, technical skill, and complete trust in the weather.

Jean-Pierre Seger and Lawrence Marais are two South African pilots who have dedicated themselves to pushing the boundaries of this extreme sport. In 2024, JP and a fellow pilot made history by flying a paramotor from Johannesburg to Cape Town—a journey many believed was impossible due to unpredictable winds and treacherous terrain, especially over the Karoo. Now, JP and Lawrence are planning an even more ambitious adventure: flying from the northernmost point of South Africa to its southernmost tip, a **1,850km journey that has never been attempted.**

The expedition is fraught with risks—turbulent wind conditions, emergency landings in remote areas, and the physical toll of flying long hours exposed to the elements. Safety is paramount, with constant navigation adjustments, fuel planning, and close coordination with a support crew on the ground.

To truly understand the appeal and the dangers, **our presenter steps into their world—strapping in, lifting off, and experiencing first-hand the exhilarating, unpredictable nature of paramotoring.** From heart-stopping takeoffs to soaring over vast landscapes, this is a journey into the unknown, where every flight is a test of skill, nerve, and resilience.

Script:


Opening Montage of Paramotoring
Wide aerial shot of a paramotor soaring through the sky at sunrise, golden light washing over the landscape.
PTC (Erin): Most of us have dreamed of flying but some choose to do it differently. No runway, no plane, just a motor on your back and a wing above. This is paramotoring.
Paramotoring Montage
Erin:
It is so beautiful up here!!!
JP: (Sit-down interview.) Paramotoring is powered paragliding. The best way to explain it is in Cape Town you'd see them flying around lion's head landing at sea point. That is called paragliding, very dependent on the wind and which way it blows. Powered paragliding is what is commonly known as paramotoring and that is a route I rather chose because I can fly at any time and I create my own lift morning, afternoon or in the evening.
VO1: Jean-Pierre Seger is no stranger to endurance. A dedicated Comrades runner and triathlete, he’s spent years pushing his limits. But another bug has bitten - paramotoring.
The motor on his back provides what is known as “lift” — getting him airborne & keeping him there.
Erin: Can you remember the first time you took off?
JP: Yeah, absolutely. It happened so quickly, you know, the lift, the thrust of the motor, the sound, it's incredibly overwhelming and I was absolutely petrified. I have to acknowledge that it was the most scary moment in my life. That didn't stop me. I carried on and I'm over 200 flights strong now and I won't stop.
VO2: But it wasn’t long before Jean-Pierre wanted to push further. Much further.
JP: I asked my instructor at the time, has anybody flown to Cape Town? And he says no, it's never been done. The Karoo’s a bit of a problem because it's so hot. And in the back of my mind I made a note, Joburg to Cape Town.
VO3: And so, in 2024 JP and a friend set off on a South African first. Paramotoring from Johannesburg to Cape Town!
On the very first day they were plagued with technical difficulties, headwinds, and what they call "motor-outs" — when the engine strapped to your back suddenly cuts out.
Luckily, when the motor dies, you don’t drop. The wing, as it’s known, keeps you gliding through the air — giving pilots time to find a safe landing spot.
The journey got off to a rough start. But they pushed on.
JP: I didn't realise how mountainous the Karoo was until the sun started rising and the sun would illuminate the top of the mountains down. It looked like everything had crowns on. I was just like, the tears just ran down my face. I don't know if that's manly enough to say. My brain couldn't comprehend how magnificent the view was.
VO4: They completed the journey of over 1,400 kilometers in 5 days, through some of the country's most unforgiving terrain. And soon after - JP started planning the next adventure.
But he had a problem… there was no one to join him.
JP: The cross-country flying is not well represented in South Africa in paramotoring. But I noticed Lawrence was doing cross-country flying. And I told him about what I wanted to do and he was like, okay.
VO5: Early the next morning, I join the guys as they prepare for lift-off. That's where I meet Lawrence Marais, ready and eager to show me the ropes.
Erin Upsounds: …But the reward, of course, is taking up into the sky.
VO6: Lawrence is key to this adventure and it quickly becomes clear why.
Lawrence Marais: I started flying with my dad from a very small age. As I grew up flying, my dad taught me. I couldn't reach the pedals at the bottom. I couldn't see over the dash. So my dad had books where I sat on and flying. And the airplane is like driving your car in the road. Flying a paramotor is going on a motorbike. You don't have a cockpit. You don't have an altimeter. You don't have anything. It's the most basic form of aviation.
VO7: And that's exactly why careful planning and training are so important.
(GAP)
JP and Lawrence take to the skies, leaving me behind. But not for long. My ride is slower but much bigger!
PTC: This isn't just for fun, every flight is crucial training. They're preparing for a brave adventure, a daring challenge and a first in paramotoring!
Lawrence: We want to fly from the most northern part of South Africa to the most southern part of South Africa with a paramotor.
Cloth, man and machine, elements, that's it. First time has been done. This flying part is as safe as you make it or as dangerous as you make it.
Flying close to your fellow paramotors is dangerous because anything can happen. And when you fly into each other, it's also a big problem.
Your equipment, everything has to be in top-notch condition. If it's not, it's dangerous.
VO8: With flight comes risk. And for Lawrence, that risk hit close to home. He lost his father in a plane crash.
Lawrence Marais: My dad was actually my buddy. We did sailing together, motorcycling together, flew together. He was a big inspiration. Every time when I get into an aeroplane, after that, I was looking for my dad. The important thing I took out of that is, to be safe. Talk on the radio. Tell the people where you are. How high, where you're going. Because that can save your life.
VO9: With safety top of mind, Lawrence has carefully mapped out the North-to-South route—but a journey this ambitious comes with plenty of obstacles.
Lawrence: I had to plan the route that we cross this mountain early in the morning, as early as possible. The problem with the Karoo weather, you get thermals, dust devils all year round. And if the wind conditions are not correct, you will have a big problem.
VO10: I want to get out of the hot air balloon and under a wing.
(GAP)
It takes months to earn a Powered Paraglider Pilot License, so I won’t be flying solo—but I am hoping to get a taste of what it is like!
Erin upsound:
“Three, two, one, go! Go. Let's go. I'm gonna go. Yes, run. Okay. And stop. That was amazing!”
VO11: After that little teaser, it's time to fly for real—in a tandem powered paraglider trike!
Hendrik upsound:
“We'll do a very mellow flight. You can tell me how far we need to take it.”
VO12: My pilot is Hendrik Theron, a former member of South Africa’s national powered paragliding team.
Erin: Well, glasses are off. Hair is going up… OK, so you've got contacts in.
Erin Bates: (Smiling.) Alright… I'm excited, but I do have a little bit of nervousness, and I think that's healthy under the circumstances. So here goes…
Erin Bates: Woo! - Oh my gosh, we're just a few seconds in the air, and it's so beautiful up here.
Hendrik SUBTITLES: Okay, so if you look over there, you can see power lines.
Erin: Yes.
Hendrik SUBTITLES: So this is one of the greatest dangers that we have when you're flying low.
Erin Bates SUBTITLES: (Excited, through comms.) You can really see why people love the sport. I mean, the views are amazing, even with the clouds. You are so in the elements as well. Being in the wind, in the clouds, it really is a special way to see our country.
JP
The accolades of being the first to fly from Joburg to Cape Town and from north to south, it's just about raising the bar. You know, how far can we go? Two or three people shouldn't just be doing that. There should be 300 people doing it, and that's what I'd like. I'm particularly ambitious to see the sport grow.
Tomorrow's not promised, and we're not going to live forever.
Erin PTC
I've had an exhilarating time getting a glimpse into the world of paramotoring, and for these guys, it's just the beginning. In May, they begin a journey that's never been done before…
VO: And I cannot wait to join them on the quest!










PROMOS
Teaser 1:
Erin: I really, I'd love to start this. No, I do. I want to.
VO:
It looks easy—a wing, a motor, and the open sky.
JP:
When I fly, it switches everything off. There's nothing else that I have enjoyed in life that comes close to this experience.
Teaser 2:
VO:
Lawrence Marais and JP Seger are chasing a paramotoring first!
Lawrence: We want to fly from the most northern part of South Africa to the most southern part of South Africa with a paramotor.
JP: There's gonna be wind, we have to get about 6,000 feet above ground!
VO: Despite the risks, they're set to take off on an epic adventure this May!
Teaser 3:
VO:
Paramotoring might seem like the ultimate freedom—but with flight comes risk.
Lawrence (verbatim):
"If the wind is not good, you can't fly. Everything has to be in top-notch condition. If it's not, it's dangerous.
VO: Even with the risks, they're gearing up for an epic adventure this May!
Teaser 4:
Erin: Joh, there's a lot of weight on this.
VO:
Paramotoring is a physical challenge, pushing endurance athletes and thrill seekers to new limits.
JP: I can go absolutely anywhere with a paramotor.
VO: Now, JP Seger faces his toughest challenge yet—flying South Africa from North to South!

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche: Strapped to a motor, lifted by a wing—meet the daring pilots pushing paramotoring to new limits, soaring where no one thought possible.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A first-hand look at the thrill and danger of cross-country paramotoring, as daring pilots defy the impossible—soaring across South Africa with nothing but a wing, a motor, and sheer determination.
metadata.Summary: **Summary:** Paramotoring—pure flight with nothing but a motor on your back and a wing above. It’s thrilling, it’s dangerous, and for a handful of South Africans, it’s an obsession. Meet Jean-Pierre Seger and Lawrence Marais, two pilots pushing the limits of what’s possible. From flying the first-ever paramotor journey from Joburg to Cape Town to planning an even greater challenge—crossing South Africa from north to south. With the sky as their only road and the wind as their greatest ally—or worst enemy—this is a test of endurance, skill, and survival. Our presenter takes to the skies to experience it firsthand, uncovering the risks, the freedom, and the sheer adrenaline of powered flight.
metadata.Further information: **Further Information:** Paramotoring is one of the most accessible forms of powered flight, requiring only a motorized backpack and a parachute-like wing to take off. But cross-country paramotoring is an entirely different challenge—demanding endurance, technical skill, and complete trust in the weather. Jean-Pierre Seger and Lawrence Marais are two South African pilots who have dedicated themselves to pushing the boundaries of this extreme sport. In 2024, JP and a fellow pilot made history by flying a paramotor from Johannesburg to Cape Town—a journey many believed was impossible due to unpredictable winds and treacherous terrain, especially over the Karoo. Now, JP and Lawrence are planning an even more ambitious adventure: flying from the northernmost point of South Africa to its southernmost tip, a **1,850km journey that has never been attempted.** The expedition is fraught with risks—turbulent wind conditions, emergency landings in remote areas, and the physical toll of flying long hours exposed to the elements. Safety is paramount, with constant navigation adjustments, fuel planning, and close coordination with a support crew on the ground. To truly understand the appeal and the dangers, **our presenter steps into their world—strapping in, lifting off, and experiencing first-hand the exhilarating, unpredictable nature of paramotoring.** From heart-stopping takeoffs to soaring over vast landscapes, this is a journey into the unknown, where every flight is a test of skill, nerve, and resilience.
